title: Totals per group
objectives: Group rows with `GROUP BY` and aggregate each group
Group by two columns and predict how many rows come back
Spot a column that is neither grouped nor aggregated

screens.title: One pile per ticker
screens.prose:
The table now holds three tickers over three days.

```sql
SELECT ticker, AVG(close)
FROM prices
GROUP BY ticker;
```
screens.question: Tap the closes that feed the `BARC` row of the result.

hints.text: What do the rows of the BARC result have in common?
Look down the ticker column for BARC.
BARC appears on rows 2, 5 and 8. Tap their closes.

feedback.correct: Three BARC rows feed the BARC average.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only rows whose ticker is BARC feed the BARC row.

byKey.all: You fed every close into one average, as in the last lesson. `GROUP BY ticker` gives each ticker its own rows.
byKey.r0c2: That is an AZN close. It feeds the AZN row of the result, not the BARC row.
byKey.r2c2: That is a SHEL close. It feeds the SHEL row of the result.

explain.text: `GROUP BY ticker` sorts the rows into one pile per ticker. BARC's pile has three rows, and `AVG` folds just those: £6.45 / 3 = £2.15.

screens.title: One row per group
screens.prose:
```sql
SELECT ticker, AVG(close)
FROM prices
GROUP BY ticker;
```
screens.question: How many rows does this query return?

options.why: You expected one result per input row. Each group folds into one row.
You folded the whole table into one value, as in the last lesson. `GROUP BY` gives one row per group.

hints.text: How many piles of rows did you need on the last screen?
There are three distinct tickers.
One pile per ticker, one row per pile.

feedback.correct: One row per ticker: AZN, BARC and SHEL.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the groups, not the rows.

explain.text: Each pile of rows sharing a ticker is a **group**. `GROUP BY` makes the groups and each aggregate summarises one, so three tickers give three rows.

screens.title: Filter, then group
screens.prose:
```sql
SELECT ticker, SUM(volume)
FROM prices
WHERE date >= '2024-03-12'
GROUP BY ticker;
```
screens.question: Tap the volumes that feed the `SHEL` row of the result.

hints.text: `WHERE` runs before the groups are made.
Only 12 and 13 March pass the date test.
SHEL rows on 12 and 13 March: tap their two volumes.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the SHEL rows that pass the date test.

byKey.no-where: You took all three SHEL days. `WHERE` drops 11 March before the groups are made.
byKey.r2c3: SHEL on 11 March fails the date test, so `WHERE` drops it before grouping.
byKey.r3c3: That is an AZN volume. It feeds the AZN row.
byKey.r4c3: That is a BARC volume. It feeds the BARC row.

explain.text: `WHERE` removes the 11 March rows first. `GROUP BY` then piles up what is left, so the SHEL group holds two rows, and `SUM` adds them.

screens.title: AZN's average
screens.question: What is AZN's `AVG(close)`? Give pounds to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Use only the AZN rows.
The AZN closes are £118.40, £119.10 and £117.60.
They add to £355.10. Divide by 3.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Average the three AZN closes only.

byKey.trunc: You cut off the digits after the second place. 118.3666... rounds up to 118.37.
byKey.sum: You added the AZN closes but did not divide by 3.
byKey.all: You averaged all nine closes. The AZN row uses only the AZN group.

explain.text: SQLite prints `118.36666666666667`, the float nearest to 355.10 / 3. `ROUND(AVG(close), 2)` turns it into `118.37`, which is what a report or a test should see.

screens.title: Average close per ticker
screens.prose: Now write it. Sort the result with `ORDER BY ticker`, so the rows always come back in the same order.
screens.question: Return each ticker with its average close rounded to 2 decimal places, sorted by ticker.

widget.solution:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE prices(date TEXT, ticker TEXT, close REAL, volume INTEGER)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO prices VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", [
    ("2024-03-11", "AZN", 118.40, 2100000),
    ("2024-03-11", "BARC", 2.12, 41000000),
    ("2024-03-11", "SHEL", 25.80, 9800000),
    ("2024-03-12", "AZN", 119.10, 1900000),
    ("2024-03-12", "BARC", 2.18, 52000000),
    ("2024-03-12", "SHEL", 26.05, 8700000),
    ("2024-03-13", "AZN", 117.60, 2600000),
    ("2024-03-13", "BARC", 2.15, 38000000),
    ("2024-03-13", "SHEL", 26.30, 9100000),
])


def query():
    return """
SELECT ticker, ROUND(AVG(close), 2)
FROM prices
GROUP BY ticker
ORDER BY ticker
"""

hints.text: Group by the column that names the piles.
You need `GROUP BY ticker`, then `ORDER BY ticker` last.
`SELECT ticker, ROUND(AVG(close), 2) FROM prices GROUP BY ticker ORDER BY ticker`

feedback.correct: Three rows, one per ticker, in a fixed order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the examples and compare your rows with the expected ones.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `[('AZN', 118.37), ('BARC', 2.15), ('SHEL', 26.05)]`. Check the grouping, the rounding and the order.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 adds HSBA. If it is missing, the query lists tickers by name instead of grouping them.

explain.text: `GROUP BY ticker` makes the groups, `AVG` folds each one, and `ROUND` fixes the floats. `ORDER BY` sorts the finished rows, so the tests can compare them exactly.

screens.title: Two columns, one group
screens.prose:
Group by two columns and each group is one pair of values.

```sql
SELECT date, ticker, COUNT(*)
FROM trades
GROUP BY date, ticker;
```
screens.question: How many rows does this return?

hints.text: List the date and ticker pairs that actually appear.
BARC trades only on 12 March.
The pairs are (12 March, AZN), (12 March, BARC) and (13 March, AZN).

feedback.correct: Three pairs appear, so three groups.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the distinct date and ticker pairs in the table.

byKey.all-pairs: You counted every date and ticker combination. BARC has no fills on 13 March, so that pair makes no group.
byKey.one-col: You grouped by one column. Each distinct pair of date and ticker is its own group.
byKey.rows: You counted fills. Each group becomes one row, however many fills it holds.

explain.text: The groups are (12 March, AZN), (12 March, BARC) and (13 March, AZN). A pair with no rows makes no group. It is missing from the result, not shown with a count of 0.

screens.title: A column with no rule
screens.prose:
A colleague wants each ticker's average with its date.

```sql
SELECT ticker, date, AVG(close)
FROM prices
GROUP BY ticker;
```
screens.question: SQLite runs this. Which date appears beside AZN?

options.text: One of AZN's three dates, and nothing says which

options.why: You expected SQL to pick the latest row. Nothing in the query asks for that, so SQLite takes whichever row it meets.

options.text: All three dates, in one cell
options.why: One group makes one row with one cell per column. Three dates cannot fit, so SQLite keeps one.

options.text: No date: SQLite refuses the query
options.why: PostgreSQL would refuse it. SQLite runs it and quietly picks a date, which is why the bug is easy to miss.

hints.text: How many dates does the AZN group hold?
The AZN group has three dates but only one row to fill.
`date` is neither in `GROUP BY` nor inside an aggregate, so no rule says which date to show.

feedback.correct: The date is arbitrary, so the query is a bug.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which rule chooses one date out of three.

byKey.last: You expected SQL to pick the latest row. Nothing in the query asks for that, so SQLite takes whichever row it meets.

explain.text: `date` is neither grouped nor aggregated, so three dates must squeeze into one cell. This SQLite printed 11 March, but nothing guarantees it. Group by the column, aggregate it with `MAX(date)`, or drop it.

canvas.caption: three dates, one cell: SQLite picks one

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose:
Every column in `SELECT` must be in `GROUP BY` or inside an aggregate. The result has one row per group that has rows.

```sql
SELECT ticker,                -- grouped
       COUNT(*),              -- aggregated
       ROUND(AVG(close), 2)   -- aggregated
FROM prices
GROUP BY ticker
ORDER BY ticker;
```
screens.question: Which `SELECT` list is safe with `GROUP BY ticker`?

options.why: `date` is neither grouped nor aggregated, so each group shows an arbitrary date.
The bare `close` is not grouped. Each group would show one arbitrary close beside its average.

feedback.correct: Every column is grouped or aggregated.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check each column against the rule.

explain.text: `ticker` is grouped, and `MIN(date)` and `MAX(close)` are aggregates. Each has exactly one value per group.

screens.title: Fix the query
screens.prose:
We want one row per ticker with its average close and its last trading date.

```sql
SELECT ticker, ____, AVG(close)
FROM prices
GROUP BY ticker;
```
screens.question: Which expression fills the gap?

options.why: A bare `date` is the bug from the last screen: SQLite shows an arbitrary date from the group.
`MIN(date)` is the first date, 11 March. We want the last one.

hints.text: The gap must give one date per group.
An aggregate turns a group of dates into one date.
ISO dates sort as text in date order, so `MAX` gives the latest.

feedback.correct: `MAX(date)` gives 13 March for every ticker here.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The gap needs one well-defined date per group.

explain.text: Dates written as `YYYY-MM-DD` sort as text in time order. So `MAX(date)` is each group's latest date, a rule rather than an accident.

ideas: `GROUP BY` sorts the rows into one group per distinct value, and every aggregate runs once per group.
Grouping by two columns makes one group per pair that actually appears; a pair with no rows is simply absent.
Every column in `SELECT` must be grouped or aggregated; `ORDER BY` fixes the order of the groups.

formula.name: Rows returned
formula.tex: \text{rows out} = \text{number of distinct groups that have rows}
formula.note: Not the number of input rows, and not every possible combination.

summary.trap: A column that is neither grouped nor aggregated shows an arbitrary value from each group; SQLite runs it without a warning.

quiz.prose:
A `prices` table holds 4 tickers with 250 trading days each: 1,000 rows.

```sql
SELECT ticker, COUNT(*)
FROM prices
GROUP BY ticker;
```
quiz.question: How many rows does this return?

feedback.correct: One row per ticker, each with a count of 250.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the groups.

byKey.rows: You counted input rows. Each group returns one row.
byKey.days: That is the count inside each row, not the number of rows.
byKey.one: One row is a whole-table aggregate. `GROUP BY ticker` gives one per ticker.

explain.text: Four tickers make four groups, so four rows come back. Each holds `COUNT(*) = 250`.

quiz.prose: You want the number of trading days for each ticker.
quiz.question: Which query gives it?

options.text: `SELECT ticker, COUNT(*) FROM prices GROUP BY ticker`

options.why: You counted the whole table: one number for all tickers together.
Without `GROUP BY` the whole table is one group. SQLite returns one row, with a ticker picked for you.

feedback.correct: Grouping by ticker gives one count per ticker.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The count must be per ticker.

explain.text: `GROUP BY ticker` makes one group per ticker, and `COUNT(*)` counts the rows in each. Without it the whole table is one group.

quiz.prose:
A `trades` table covers 5 days and 4 tickers. One ticker was suspended for 2 of the days and has no fills then. Every other ticker traded every day.

```sql
SELECT date, ticker, SUM(qty)
FROM trades
GROUP BY date, ticker;
```
quiz.question: How many rows does this return?

feedback.correct: 20 possible pairs, minus the 2 with no fills: 18.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the date and ticker pairs that have at least one fill.

byKey.all-pairs: You counted every pair. The suspended ticker has no rows on 2 days, so those pairs make no group.
byKey.sum: You added the days and the tickers. Each group is one pair of a day and a ticker.

explain.text: Five days times four tickers is 20 pairs. Two pairs have no rows, and a pair with no rows makes no group, so 18 rows come back.

quiz.prose: Each query below ends with `GROUP BY ticker`.
quiz.question: Which one shows a value that SQL does not define?

options.why: Both closes are aggregated, so each group has exactly one of each.
`COUNT(close)` is an aggregate. It counts the closes present in each group.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a column outside `GROUP BY` and outside any aggregate.

explain.text: A bare `close` beside `GROUP BY ticker` has several values per group and no rule to pick one. Every other column here is grouped or aggregated.
